units.name: matcher-interface
units.role: The shared contract every pattern engine must satisfy, plus the value types the whole pipeline passes around.
units.description: This is the common language every pattern-search engine in ripgrep must speak, without doing any searching itself. It defines what a match is (a start and end position inside a chunk of bytes), what a line ending is (a chosen byte, or the two-byte Windows pair), and a compact table recording which bytes can never appear inside a match so faster strategies can be chosen. Its centrepiece is a contract listing everything an engine can be asked to do: find the first match from a position, walk every non-overlapping match, report capture groups, say whether it is line-oriented, and offer a cheap 'this line might match' hint that may raise a false alarm but must never miss a real match. It also expands replacement templates like $1 and $name from captured text. It never opens files or knows how results are printed.

units.name: regex-matcher
units.role: Compiles patterns plus options into a matcher backed by Rust's regex engine, with literal extraction and line-terminator safety.
units.description: This is ripgrep's default pattern engine. It takes the pattern text a user typed plus the switches that change its meaning (case handling, whole-word, whole-line, plain-text, multiline, CRLF, Unicode, size limits) and produces a ready-to-use matcher. It reasons about the pattern three ways. For smart case it inspects the pattern for uppercase letters before deciding to ignore case. When searching is line-oriented it rewrites the pattern so it can never match across a line break, refusing with a clear error if the user explicitly asked for a newline rather than silently changing their intent. And it extracts plain literal strings hidden inside the pattern to build a cheap secondary pattern, so most lines are skipped fast and only promising ones run the full pattern. It also rejects patterns needing a byte the caller declared impossible, such as NUL. Every shortcut may raise a false alarm that is then verified, but must never lose a genuine match.

units.name: pcre2-matcher
units.role: A PCRE2-backed implementation of the same matcher contract, for patterns the default engine cannot express.
units.description: This is the second, interchangeable pattern engine. It wraps the PCRE2 library, which understands a richer pattern language than the default engine, including back-references and look-around. Its job is to translate ripgrep's user-facing options -- case sensitivity, smart case, plain-text patterns, whole-word, whole-line, multiline, CRLF, Unicode awareness, and an optional just-in-time compiler for speed -- into PCRE2's own settings, combine several patterns into one, compile them, and report where matches begin and end plus the positions of capture groups. It presents exactly the same contract as the default engine so the searching, printing and counting parts of ripgrep never need to know which engine is in play. It must never read files, print output, or decide which files to search, and must report a clean error rather than crash when a pattern is invalid or too large.

units.name: glob-matching
units.role: Compiles shell-style wildcard patterns into matchers and multi-pattern sets, and matches paths against them.
units.description: This unit reads shell-style file patterns and turns them into fast tests answering 'does this file path match?'. It parses the pattern text, reports precise human-readable errors for malformed patterns such as an unclosed bracket or an inverted range, and compiles each pattern into the cheapest possible plan: a plain string comparison, a file-extension lookup, a prefix or suffix check, or, only when necessary, a full regular expression. It can also bundle many patterns into one set checked against a path in a single pass, reporting every pattern that matched at once, which is what makes checking thousands of ignore rules per file affordable. It normalizes path separators so a pattern behaves the same on Windows and Unix. It is pure computation: it never touches the file system, never asks whether a path exists, and never decides policy about which files should be searched.

units.name: gitignore-rules
units.role: Parses gitignore-style rule files and command-line globs into ignore/whitelist/no-opinion decisions.
units.description: This is the rule book for deciding which files a search should skip. It reads the ignore lists people write by hand and the glob patterns typed on the command line, and turns each line into a matcher. It implements git's exact conventions: a later rule beats an earlier one, a leading exclamation mark un-ignores something, a trailing slash restricts a rule to directories, a leading slash anchors a rule to the folder its ignore file lives in, a hash starts a comment, and a bare name matches at any depth. Given a path it answers one of three things: skip it, explicitly keep it, or no opinion. It also locates git's user-wide ignore file by reading git config files and environment variables. The same machinery, with the exclamation mark's meaning flipped, implements the user's own include and exclude globs. It must never shell out to git, and never decide anything the rules did not say.

units.name: file-type-filter
units.role: Owns the named file-type vocabulary and decides whether a path is selected or excluded by type.
units.description: This unit holds ripgrep's vocabulary of named file types and decides, for any file, whether it is one the user asked to search. It knows that 'rust' means files ending in .rs and that 'cpp' means .cc, .hpp, .cxx and friends, and it ships a large built-in catalogue of roughly a thousand such names. Users can extend or replace the catalogue on the command line by adding a definition, composing existing types into a new one, or clearing a type entirely, and can then say which types they want and which they do not. The unit compiles the chosen names into a fast filename matcher and answers one question per path: explicitly wanted, explicitly excluded, or not covered by any rule. It also exposes the full list of names and patterns so ripgrep can print them. It never reads a file's contents to guess its type; the decision comes purely from the name.

units.name: directory-walker
units.role: Recursive, ignore-aware traversal, plus the shared error/match vocabulary and path helpers of the ignore crate.
units.description: This is the part of ripgrep that answers 'which files should we actually look at?'. Given one or more starting directories it walks everything underneath, either one file at a time or spread across worker threads. As it descends it keeps a running stack of the ignore rules that apply at each level, so a rule written in a parent folder still governs files deep inside child folders. It enforces the practical limits a user asks for: how deep to go, whether to include hidden files, whether to follow symbolic links and how to detect loops, skipping files above a size limit, staying on one filesystem, and never searching ripgrep's own output stream. Surviving files are handed back one by one along with any errors met. It also offers an incremental mode that answers 'would this single path have been ignored?' without traversing, loading only the ignore files needed. It owns the three-way ignore/whitelist/no-opinion answer and the error type the rule and type filters both speak.

units.name: search-input-reader
units.role: Gets a file's bytes in front of the search engine, by memory map or by a growable line-aligned buffer.
units.description: This is the part that actually gets the bytes of a file in front of the pattern matcher. It offers two ways. The first is memory mapping: asking the operating system to expose an entire file as if it were already in memory, which is fast but only done when the caller has explicitly opted in and the platform benefits, falling back quietly to normal reading if mapping fails. The second is a streaming buffer: it reads a chunk of a file or pipe into a reusable block of memory, then hands out only the portion ending at the last complete line, keeping any half-finished line hidden until more data arrives. When a single line is too long to fit, the buffer grows, either without limit or up to a configured cap after which it reports an error. Leftover bytes roll to the front between reads and running byte counts are tracked so matches are reported at their true position. It also performs the byte-level binary-file check, either stopping at a marker byte or replacing it with a line break.

units.role: Runs a matcher over one haystack line by line or across lines, and pushes results to a caller-supplied sink.
units.description: This is the part of ripgrep that looks through the contents of one file or stream. Given a matcher and a haystack it decides where each line starts and ends, asks the matcher whether a line matches, and hands every result to whoever asked. It implements the behaviours people expect from a grep-like tool: showing lines that do not match, showing a few lines before and after each hit, marking the gaps between separated groups of context, echoing every line in passthru mode, counting line numbers, stopping early once enough matches are found or the file looks like binary junk, and converting text from other character encodings into UTF-8 before searching. Results are not returned as a list: the unit calls back into a caller-supplied receiver for each match, each context line, the start of a search and a final summary. units.description: This unit decides how ripgrep's results look on screen and how they link back to the files they came from. units.description: This is the part of ripgrep that turns raw search results into the text a person actually sees. It knows the familiar grep layout: an optional file name, a line number, a column number, a byte offset, the matching line itself, and separators between blocks of context. It can highlight matched words in color, replace matched text with something else, print only the matched fragment rather than the whole line, trim leading whitespace, and shorten very long lines with a short preview instead of dumping thousands of characters. units.name: json-output
units.role: Serializes search results into ripgrep's documented JSON Lines wire format.
units.description: This unit turns search results into machine-readable JSON instead of human-readable text. As ripgrep searches a file it emits a stream of small records, one per line: a begin record when a file starts being searched, a match record for each matching line carrying the line text, line number, byte offset and the exact start and end positions of each matched piece plus replacement text if configured, a context record for neighbouring lines shown around matches, and an end record with summary statistics such as elapsed time, bytes searched, bytes printed and match counts. Because JSON can only carry valid text, any line or file path that is not valid UTF-8 is emitted as base64-encoded bytes under a different key rather than as text, so tools consuming the output never receive corrupted or silently lossy data. Keeping this format stable is the point of the unit: other programs script around it.

units.name: cli-flags
units.role: Defines every ripgrep command-line flag and parses argv plus the config file into a validated settings record.
units.description: This unit is ripgrep's command-line dictionary and door-keeper. It holds the single authoritative description of every flag the tool accepts: its long name, its short name, any aliases, any negated form, whether it takes a value, which help section it belongs to, its short and long documentation, and the code that records the user's choice. It then reads what the user actually typed, and unless told not to also reads extra default flags from a settings file whose location comes from an environment variable, prepending them to the typed arguments. It resolves negations and aliases, reports unknown flags with 'did you mean' suggestions, short-circuits immediately for help and version, and produces a plain validated record of every setting. That record, together with the small vocabulary of choice types it defines for search mode, color choice, context, sorting, binary handling, encoding, pattern sources and file-type changes, is what the rest of ripgrep reads. Because the flag table is the only source of truth, help text and completions can never drift from it.

units.description: This is ripgrep's decision-making layer, sitting between the raw list of options the user typed and the machinery that does the work. It takes the parsed flags and turns them into real, ready-to-use equipment: it decides which regular-expression engine to build and how to configure it for case sensitivity, word boundaries, multiline and line-ending handling; it builds the file reader with the right context lines, encoding and memory-map strategy; it picks which kind of printer to use and how it should be colored, hyperlinked and separated; it assembles the directory walker with its hidden-file, ignore, file-type and glob rules; and it resolves the many interactions between flags, such as whether line numbers are shown, how many threads to use, whether to sort results, whether to guess the current directory or read from a pipe, and where the patterns themselves come from. units.name: search-orchestrator
units.role: Drives ripgrep end to end: mode selection, the walk, per-file search execution, statistics, warnings and exit code.
units.description: This is what actually runs when you type rg at a terminal. It starts the program, asks the argument-parsing code what the user wants, and picks a lane: search files for a pattern, just list the files that would be searched, list the known file types, print help or version, or generate documentation and shell completions. For searching it walks the directory tree either one file at a time or across many threads, turns each entry into a haystack worth searching while skipping directories and broken entries, and hands each one to a search worker. The worker decides how to reach the file's contents -- read it directly, memory-map it, read standard input, run a user-supplied preprocessor program, or pipe it through a decompressor -- then pairs the chosen engine with the chosen output format. It tallies match counts and statistics, times the run, prints a warning if it suspects an ignore rule silently filtered everything away, and chooses the exit code. It also owns the small shared switchboard controlling whether warnings print at all and the debug logger, and the umbrella library facade through which it reaches every other unit.

units.name: search-index
units.role: Opt-in on-disk ngram index store, the regex-to-ngram query analyzer, and the feature-gated shim reaching them.
units.description: This is ripgrep's experimental, opt-in search index: a side database remembering which files contain which small pieces of text, so a later search can skip files that could not possibly match. It has three parts. A small library finds or creates an index directory, consulting an environment variable and otherwise walking up from the working directory looking for a marker folder, then opening or creating a database file inside it in read-only or read-write mode. A regex analyzer takes an already-parsed pattern and works out the short character sequences any matching file must contain, expressed as a tree of and/or conditions. And a tiny switch inside the ripgrep program exposes two functions, build and use, which exist in two versions so the build can pick the real one when the feature is enabled and a version that simply reports 'not enabled in this build' otherwise. The plumbing is deliberately incomplete: opening the database works, but the index is not yet consulted, so an indexed search still falls back to reading every file.

units.description: This is the toolbox of small conveniences a command-line search program needs to behave politely toward whoever runs it. It figures out whether input is being piped in or typed at a keyboard, and whether output is going to a terminal or being redirected into a file; that decision determines whether results are flushed line by line so a human sees them immediately, or in larger faster chunks better suited to a file. It provides a colored output stream wrapper that hides which buffering strategy is in use. It handles awkward text: turning arbitrary raw bytes into a readable, typeable form and back again, so unprintable characters can be shown in messages or entered as arguments. It reads search patterns from a file or from piped input one per line, reporting the exact file, line number and byte offset when a pattern is not valid text. And it parses friendly size strings into an exact number of bytes and asks the operating system for the machine's hostname.

units.name: process-decompression
units.role: Runs an external program as a child process and streams its output as file contents, chiefly for compressed files.
units.description: This unit lets ripgrep search inside compressed files without understanding any compression format itself. It keeps a table mapping file name patterns to an external helper program and its arguments, so that for example gzip-compressed files are handed to the gzip program. Before using a helper it looks the program up in the system search path so a full unambiguous path is used, which avoids accidentally running a stray program from the current directory. When a matching file is found it launches the helper as a separate child process, feeds it the file, and hands the helper's output back as if it were the plain contents of the file. If no rule matches, or the helper is not installed, it quietly falls back to reading the raw file. It also solves a general plumbing problem: while streaming a child's output, anything the child writes to its error channel is drained on a background thread so the child can never block and freeze the search, and a failing child's error text becomes a readable message rather than silent corruption.

violations_observed.note: The ignore crate's shared vocabulary (Error, Match, PartialErrorBuilder) and the path helpers live in lib.rs and pathutil.rs, which this manifest assigns to directory-walker. The rule and type filters import them directly, so directory-walker is simultaneously a consumer of gitignore-rules and the owner of the types gitignore-rules returns. A cleaner split would lift the shared vocabulary into its own unit.

The JSON printer reaches into crate-private helpers of the human printer (CounterWriter, Stats, Replacer, find_iter_at_in_context) rather than through any exported API. They are listed as match-printer entrypoints here so the edge resolves, but they are internals, not a designed interface.

The hyperlink code borrows DecimalFormatter, a crate-private number-formatting helper owned by match-printer, while match-printer simultaneously depends on output-styling. The dependency between the two printer halves runs both ways.

crates/core/flags/mod.rs is a shared roof: it owns the Flag trait and Category but also declares the hiargs, doc and complete modules and re-exports their functions, so the config-assembly and doc-generation units reach the outside world through a file this unit owns, and parse.rs calls HiArgs::from_low_args directly.

The index shim calls back into the orchestrator's search and search_parallel functions while the orchestrator calls index::read and index::write, making the dependency circular. Those two functions are listed as orchestrator entrypoints so the edge resolves.

crates/cli/src/lib.rs is the only declaration site for the decompress and process modules and re-exports their public items, so the file assigned to cli-support-utils is what makes process-decompression reachable at all.

crates/grep/src/lib.rs is a six-line umbrella crate of re-exports aggregating six units and belonging naturally to none. It is assigned to search-orchestrator because the crates/core files are its only in-repo consumers, but it is really a packaging facade rather than orchestration logic.
